en: The Gopālatāpinī Upaniṣad The glorious abode of the five words, resplendent with its specific attributes.
I worship Hari, who is free from all counter-correlates and devoid of distinctions.
Oṃ. May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O worshipful ones.
With steady limbs and bodies, having offered praise, may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unbroken, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.
The Gopālatāpana, Kṛṣṇa, Yājñavalkya, Varāhaka, Śāṭyāyanī, Hayagrīva, Dattātreya, and the Gāruḍa.
Hari Om! Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, whose actions are effortless;
salutations to the Guru, who is known through the Vedānta and who is the witness of the intellect.
The sages indeed said to the Brāhmaṇa: "Who is the supreme deity? From what does death fear?
By the knowledge of what does everything become known? By what does this universe transmigrate?
To that, the Brāhmaṇa replied: "Kṛṣṇa is indeed the supreme divinity."
Death fears Govinda. Through the knowledge of Gopījanavallabha, this is understood:
"Svāhā, this entire universe wanders [in saṃsāra]. Regarding that, they said: "Who is Kṛṣṇa? Who is this Govinda? Who is Gopījanavallabha? And who is Svāhā? To them the Brāhmaṇa replied:

The remover of evil, known as the cow, the earth, and the Veda, the impeller of the collection of sciences for the cowherd folk, and His Māyā—all this is indeed the Supreme Brahman alone. He who meditates upon Him, tastes Him, and worships Him becomes immortal. They said: "What is that form? What is the tasting? Or what is it?"

"Tell me all about that worship for those who desire to know it. To this, Hairaṇya replied: "It is the cowherd's attire, free from delusion, resting upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa). Regarding this, there are these verses:"

The Lord has eyes like beautiful white lotuses, possesses the luster of a cloud, and wears garments of lightning; he is two-armed, endowed with the gesture of wisdom (jñānamudrā), and adorned with a garland of forest flowers. || 1 ||
Surrounded by cowherds, cowherdesses, and cattle, seated beneath a celestial tree,
adorned with divine ornaments, and situated in the midst of a jewel-lotus.
By meditating in one's mind upon Kṛṣṇa, who is served by breezes mingling with the waves of the waters of the Yamunā, one is liberated from the cycle of worldly existence. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, his tongue is the meeting point of water and earth. Reciting the five-word mantra— one word being *kāmādi kṛṣṇāya*, the second *govindāya*, the third *gopījana*, the fourth *vallabha*,
and the fifth *svāhā*— while reciting these five words, he [protects] the five limbs of heaven and earth.
The sun and the moon attain Brahman by means of that very form. Regarding this, there is this verse:
"Having first uttered *klīm*, one should recite *kṛṣṇāya govindāya gopījanavallabhāya* as composed by Vyāsa of the Great Manu; for him who does so, there is swift liberation, and no other."

"His goal would be attained. Devotion (*bhakti*) is his worship. This consists in fixing the mind upon him through freedom from desire for the conditions of this world or the next. And this alone is "actionlessness" (*naiṣkarmya*).
The wise worship that Kṛṣṇa in many ways.
They worship Govinda, who is peaceful, in many ways.
He who is beloved by the cowherd women, whose seed is the gods, and who rests upon the Svāhā, sustains these worlds and this entire universe. || 1 ||
Just as the single wind, having entered the world, assumes five forms among various beings,
so too Kṛṣṇa, though one, [assumes many forms] for the sake of the welfare of the world.
By means of sound, this five-footed one shines forth. Thus [it is said].

They said, "Tell us the method of worship for this Supreme Self, Govinda, the support of all. He said to them: "His seat is a golden lotus with eight petals; within that is a pair of fire-arms; within that is the primordial syllable, the seed of all, [ending] with 'Kṛṣṇāya'."

Having taken up the Brāhmaṇa [text] enriched with the seed-syllable *namaḥ*, together with Brahmā, and having duly inscribed the *Anaṅga-gāyatrī* upon a circle of the earth encircled by tridents, he arranged it surrounded by the limbs (*aṅga*),
Vāsudeva and others, his own Śaktis such as Rukmiṇī and others, Nanda and others, Vasudeva and others, the sons of Pṛthā and others, and the treasures (*nidhi*) and others.

One should worship during the twilights with acts of devotion and ritual services; by that, everything becomes accomplished for him—everything indeed becomes accomplished. Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The one controller, all-pervading, dark-hued, worthy of praise..."
Though being one, he who shines forth as many—he is the Pīṭha. Those wise ones who devote themselves to him attain eternal perfection, and no others. || 3 ||
The eternal among the eternals, the consciousness of the conscious, the one among the many who ordains their desires—
those wise ones who worship Him seated upon the throne.
For them there is eternal happiness, and not for others. || 4 ||
Those who, ever-striving and not out of desire, worship this supreme abode of Viṣṇu—
for them, He, in the form of a cowherd, [reveals Himself] through their effort.
One should reveal that very state of one's own self.
To him who created Brahmā in the beginning, and who protected the Vidyā for him— that Lord Kṛṣṇa,
the light of self-knowledge— [I bow].
One who desires liberation should go for refuge.
To those who recite the five-word mantra of Govinda interspersed with the syllable Oṃ,
He reveals His own form.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should practice constant tranquility. || 7 ||
From this very fivefold [lineage] arose the Manavas of Govinda among men;
they too, beginning with Daśārṇa, were [descended] from Saṃkrandana and the others.
They are practiced correctly by those desiring prosperity. || 8 ||
They asked him, and he said: "While I was wandering in the abode of Brahmā, the Supreme Lord was meditated upon and praised by me;
at the end of a *parārdha*, He became aware [of my devotion]. Then a Person, the teacher of knowledge, appeared before me. Thereupon, I bowed down to Him who is favorable toward His devotees."

Having bestowed upon me, for the sake of creation, the form of the eighteen-syllable mantra through my heart, He vanished. Then, as I desired to create once more, those syllables appeared before me; by dividing them among those syllables, I manifested the form of the future universe.
Thus, from the earth [arose] fire at one time, from the drop (bindu) the moon, and from their union the sun;
from the syllable *klīm* arose the eternal Kṛṣṇa, from space (kha) the wind, and from the north the fragrant sciences (*vidyās*).
"I have manifested," "I have manifested"—from that [arose] the distinction between female, male, and so forth.
"This entire [world] is this; this entire [world] is this. || 3 ||

By the sacrifice of this very [mantra], Candradhvaja, having dispelled delusion, makes himself known. One should repeat the mantra beginning with Oṃ. Free from attachment, he attained [realization]. "The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky."
Therefore, one should constantly repeat this; one should constantly cause it to revolve. ||4||
Regarding this, some say: "From the first foot [of the mantra] comes the earth, from the second foot water, from the third foot fire, from the fourth foot wind, and from the final foot space.
This is the Vaiṣṇava mantra consisting of the five *vyāhṛtis*, which illuminates Kṛṣṇa.
One should constantly repeat this for the sake of attaining isolation; one should constantly repeat it. || 5 ||
Regarding this, there are these verses: From its first part the earth arose; from the second, that which is born of water;
from the third, fire was produced; and from the fourth, the wind. (1)
One should practice that very same fifth, the arising from the sky;
thus Candradhvaja went to Viṣṇu’s supreme, imperishable state.
Then that very state, which consists of five steps, is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, and devoid of all attachment such as greed.
That Vāsudeva, than whom nothing else exists. || 3 ||

I, along with the hosts of Maruts, shall constantly praise with the supreme hymn that one Govinda, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who consists of five parts, and who sits beneath the fragrant trees of Vṛndāvana.
Oṃ, salutations again and again to Govinda, who is the universal form, the cause of the preservation and dissolution of the universe, the Lord of the universe, and the universe itself. || 1 ||
Homage to Him whose form is consciousness, whose nature is supreme bliss;
salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Gopīs, Govinda. || 2 ||
Homage to the lotus-eyed one; homage to the one garlanded with lotuses; homage to the one whose navel is a lotus; homage to the lord of Kamalā. 3.
Salutations again and again to Govinda, who is delightful with a crest of peacock feathers, whose intellect is unimpeded, and who is the swan in the lake of Ramā’s mind. || 4 ||
Salutation to the destroyer of the lineage of Kaṃsa, to the slayer of Keśin and Cāṇūra, to the one worthy of praise by the bull-bannered god, and to the charioteer of Arjuna. || 5 ||
To the cowherd who delights in the sound of the flute, the crusher of serpents,
who wanders along the banks of the Yamunā, and who wears swinging earrings.
Salutations again and again to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who wears a garland upon his lotus-like face which is like a sprout, who is skilled in the art of dance, and who protects those who bow before him. || 7 ||
Salutation to the destroyer of sins, to the upholder of Govardhana,
to the ender of Pūtanā’s life, and to the taker of Tṛṇāvarta’s breath.
Salutations again and again to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is partless, free from delusion, pure, the enemy of impurity, non-dual, and the Great One. || 9 ||
Be gracious, O Supreme Bliss; be gracious, O Supreme Lord.
O Master, lift me up, for I have been bitten by the serpent of mental and physical afflictions.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, beloved of Rukmiṇī, who captivates the hearts of the gopīs;
O Teacher of the World, lift me up, for I am submerged in the ocean of worldly existence. 11.
O Keśava, remover of afflictions, O Nārāyaṇa, O Janārdana!
O Govinda, supreme bliss, O Mādhava, lift me up!

Then, having propitiated me thus with hymns of praise, Hiraṇyagarbha said: "In that way, you shall cross over the cycle of worldly existence by chanting this five-word mantra while meditating upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Whoever should worship that five-word mantra...
"That state goes effortlessly to that alone; it is motionless, one, swifter than the mind. Even the gods did not attain it, for it moved before them. Therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme deity;
one should meditate upon him, one should savor him, one should sacrifice to him, and one should worship him.
Āūṃ. That is the Truth. Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones.
With steady limbs and bodies, having offered praise, may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unbroken, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the Gopālapūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad.
Oṃ. Once, after spending the night with longing desire, the women of Vraja spoke to Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd and Lord of All. Kṛṣṇa said to them, "Alms should be given to such-and-such a Brahmin."
"Regarding Durvāsas: how shall we cross the waters of the Yamunā?
For by saying 'O Kṛṣṇa, O Brahmacārī,' he will grant you passage—by remembering me, even the unfathomable becomes fathomable."
Remembering me, the impure becomes pure; remembering me, the one who has not taken vows becomes one who has taken vows; remembering me, the one with desires becomes free from desire;
remembering me, the one who is not learned in the Vedas becomes learned in the Vedas—me, [remembering whom...]
Having remembered that all rivers, though naturally bottomless and devoid of touch,
become shallow upon remembering that fierce speech; indeed, having heard those words, and having crossed by means of that speech,
he went to the most meritorious hermitage of Saurya and paid homage to the sage.
"For it is indeed most excellent and belongs to Rudra. Having given this to the brahmin—
consisting of milk and consisting of ghee, for it is indeed most desired and most refined—
he, being satisfied, bathed, ate, gave away the remainder, and having offered the food and recognized its nature, he gave it.
"How shall we go, having crossed the Saurī river? He, the sage, said:
"Remembering me, Durvāsas will grant you the path. Among them, Gāndharvī, the most excellent, spoke thus to him on their behalf: "How indeed [shall this be], O Kṛṣṇa?"
The student: How is the sage Durvāsana?

For they, having first established that as primary and subsequently imitated it, remained silent. Space possesses sound; [space] is distinct from both sound and space. Space resides in that; it resides in space.
For that ether does not know it; for that is the Self.
How can I be an enjoyer? This light possesses form and is distinct from both form and fire. Fire abides within it; fire abides in fire; fire [knows] it.
He does not know; for he is the Self. How can I be an enjoyer? Water, though possessing taste, is distinct from taste; it abides within those waters.
Earth, though possessing smell, is distinct from smell and earth; it abides within that earth.
It stands upon the earth; the earth does not know it, for that is the Self. [The Self thinks: "How am I a enjoyer? For this mind alone perceives this, and this mind alone grasps those [objects].
But where everything has become the Self alone, there how could one perceive, or how could one go?

For that is the Self. How can I be the enjoyer? For this Kṛṣṇa, who is most beloved, is the cause of the two bodies. There are two birds belonging to Brahman; thus, I am one, while the other becomes the enjoyer. For the other is indeed the witness.
It exists. Those two abide in the nature of the tree; therefore, they are the enjoyer and the non-enjoyer.

For the former is the enjoyer, while the other is the non-enjoyer, being Kṛṣṇa. Wherein we do not perceive knowledge and ignorance—how can he who is distinct from knowledge and ignorance, consisting of pure knowledge, be an object?

Thus it is said: "He who indeed desires objects of desire through desire becomes one possessed by desire. He who indeed desires objects of desire without desire becomes free from desire. This one, distinct from birth and old age, is the immovable pillar; he is the one who cannot be cut, who dwells in the sun, who is that [one]."
"He stands among the cows; he who protects the cowherds; he who stands among all the gods;
he who is praised by all the gods; he who, having entered into all beings, ordains all beings—he indeed becomes your master. Thus spoke Gāndharvī.
O Sage, how was this cowherd born among us, and how was this Kṛṣṇa known by you?
What is his mantra, and what is his abode? How was he born of Devakī?
Who is his wife and village? What kind of worship is there for this cowherd? He is the manifest primordial nature (prakṛti).
"How indeed did this Supreme Self, Gopāla, descend upon the earth?

To him, that daughter of a Gandharva spoke to the sage. He said to her: "Formerly, from the heart-lotus of Nārāyaṇa—in whom all worlds are woven like warp and woof—the Lotus-born One was born; having performed intense austerities,"

He granted him a boon. He chose the right to ask any question he desired. He granted it to him. Then the Lotus-born One said: "Among all the incarnations (*avatāra*), which one is the most excellent? By which do the worlds become satisfied? Remembering whom are they liberated?"
They arise from this saṃsāra. Or how does the Brahman-nature of this incarnation come about?
He said: "Indeed, that is the god Nārāyaṇa. Just as there are seven cities on the peak of Meru that are with desire (sakāmyā), so too are those without desire (niṣkāmyā) and those with desire."

In the wheel of the earth-protector (Gopāla), there are seven cities. Among them, Gopālapurī is the manifest abode of Brahman. It belongs to all the gods and all beings, whether they possess desires or are free from them. Now follows its worship, just as indeed in a lake...

The lotus stands there, and likewise it stands upon the ground. Mathurā is protected by the discus; therefore it is the City of the Cowherds (Gopālapurī). There is Bṛhad-bṛhadvana, Madhu’s Madhuvana, Tāla’s Tālavana, Kāmya’s Kāmyavana, Bahula’s Bahulavana, and Kumuda.
The city is surrounded by these: Kumudavana, Khadira, Khadiravana, Bhadra, Bhadravana, Bhāṇḍīra—namely Bhāṇḍīravana, Śrīvana, Lohavana, and Vṛndāvana.
There, within those very celestial realms, dwell gods, humans, Gandharvas, and Nāgas.
Kinnaras sing and dance there. Therein are the twelve Ādityas, the eleven Rudras, the eight Vasus, the seven Munis, Brahmā, and Nārada; and the five Vināyakas:
Vīreśvara, Rudreśvara, Ambikeśvara, Gaṇeśvara, Nīlakaṇṭheśvara, and Viśveśvara.
Gopāleśvara and Bhadreśvara—these eight, along with others, make twenty-four *liṅgas*.
There are two forests: Kṛṣṇavana and Bhadravana. Between them are twelve sacred and most meritorious forests; in those very places dwell the gods and the *siddhas* who have attained perfection.

For there, Rāma’s form is the form of Rāma, Pradyumna’s form is the form of Pradyumna, Aniruddha’s form is the form of Aniruddha, and Kṛṣṇa’s form is the form of Kṛṣṇa. Thus, there are twelve forms in the forests and likewise in Mathurā. Indeed, Rudra worships one; Brahmā worships the second.
They worship the third [tithi] as born of Brahmā; they worship the fourth as the Maruts; they worship the fifth as the Vināyakas;
and they worship the sixth as the Vasus. The sages worship the seventh; the Apsarases worship the ninth; the tenth indeed stands in concealment; and the eleventh—
She follows her own path; she abides on the twelfth stage (*bhūmi*). Indeed, those who worship her cross over death;
they attain liberation. They cross over the suffering consisting of the threefold affliction—namely, that of the womb, birth, old age, and death. On this matter, there are also these verses:
Having reached the beautiful Mathurā, which is eternally worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, and which is protected by the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the club; || 1 ||
Therein is situated that Lord Kṛṣṇa,
who, together with his powers, is concentrated along with Ramā, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Rukmiṇī.

The word "catuḥ" (four) becomes one, for the syllable *oṃ* is thus declared. From that very [syllable], [one proceeds] with "paraḥ rajase" (beyond passion). Having thus determined the Self as "so 'ham" (that am I), one should contemplate "I am Gopāla. He attains liberation; he reaches the state of Brahman; he becomes a knower of Brahman.

He brings forth the cowherds and those who live by them as His own self until the end of creation. That Gopāla is indeed *Oṃ*. *Tatsat so ’ham* (That Truth, He am I). The Supreme Brahman, whose nature is Kṛṣṇa, whose essential form is eternal bliss and unity—He am I. *Tatsad gopālo ’ham eva* (That Truth, the Cowherd, I alone am). The Supreme...

Taking as his own self the truth that is uncontradicted—"I am He"—one should effect unity with the mind. One should contemplate the Self, thinking, "I am Gopāla. That very one is the unmanifest, infinite, and eternal Gopāla.
O Brahman, my residence shall always be in Mathurā.
Indeed, [he is the one] who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, and the forest garland. || 1 ||
He who, whether situated in the region of Mathurā or even in Jambūdvīpa, [meditates upon] the universal form, the supreme light, whose true nature is devoid of form; || 2 ||
He who worships both my image and me is most dear to me on earth; established within that image in the form of Kṛṣṇa, I am to be worshipped by you always.
And according to the fourfold distinction of their entry [into the path], the people of this world who follow the ages and possess great wisdom worship me here through sacrifice.
He is Gopāla with his younger brothers, Kṛṣṇa, and Rukmiṇī; he is intent upon that.
"I am Gopāla, the unborn and eternal; I am Pradyumna, the ancient one. (5)
"I am Rāma; I am Aniruddha. Thus the wise man should worship himself according to the desireless dharma taught by me, part by part.
Indeed, I am to be worshipped by those inhabitants of Bhadrakṛṣṇa;
for those who have fallen away from that path of dharma are solely devoted to me.
Those who have indeed been swallowed by Kali have their abode in that [place],
just as you are with your sons, and just as Rudra is with his attendants.
"As one who is endowed with glory, so is my devotee dear to me.
Then the Lotus-born One said: "How can there be one God among four gods?
How has that which is renowned as the single imperishable (akṣara) come to be manifold?"
He said: "In the beginning, indeed, there was that one alone, Brahman, without a second. From that came the unmanifest, the single syllable (akṣara). From that syllable came the Great (mahat).
From the Great came the ego (ahaṅkāra). From that ego came the five subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi)."
From them [arose] the elements; by them the Imperishable is enveloped.
The Imperishable is I, this *oṃkāra*, which is undecaying, immortal, fearless, and deathless—Brahman, for it is indeed fearlessness. I am liberated; I am the Imperishable.
It is pure existence, the very nature of consciousness, luminous, and all-pervading. || 9 ||
Brahman is indeed one and non-dual, yet through *māyā* it appears as a fourfold [manifestation].
Rohiṇī’s son, Viśva, is born from the syllable *a*.
Pradyumna, whose nature is taijasa, arises from the syllable 'U'; Aniruddha, whose nature is prājña, arises from the syllable 'M'.
Kṛṣṇa, whose nature consists of half a mora, in whom the universe is established;
and Rukmiṇī, who is identical with Kṛṣṇa, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) and the creator of the world. 12.
Born from the women of Vraja and conjoined with knowledge through the Vedas,
the exponents of Brahman declare his state as Prakṛti by virtue of being the Praṇava.
Therefore, Gopāla, who is established as the universe, is born from the syllable Oṃ;
the exponents of Brahman declare that Klīm is the single reality of the syllable Oṃ.
By meditating especially upon me in Mathurā, one attains liberation;
there, the eight-petaled heart-lotus is fully blossomed and situated.
His two feet were marked with divine banners and parasols;
his chest bore the Śrīvatsa emblem, and he was endowed with the radiant Kaustubha gem.
Four-armed, equipped with the conch, discus, bow, lotus, and mace;
his arms adorned with beautiful armlets and his neck graced by a splendid garland.
He wears a radiant crown, is fearless, and has shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings;
he possesses a golden and gentle form, bestowing fearlessness upon his own devotee.
One should constantly meditate in the mind upon me as the bearer of the flute and horn,
or upon that by which the entire world is churned through the knowledge of Brahman.
Whatever constitutes my essence is called Mathurā;
by the eight guardians of the directions, this lotus of the earth has been made to blossom throughout the world.
Born from the ocean of saṃsāra, it was served within my mind;
there were divine banners with the luster of the moon and sun, and Mount Meru made of gold.
The parasol is remembered as the Brahma-world, and the foot is situated above it;
the nature of the Śrīvatsa exists together with its characteristic marks.
Therefore, it is called the Śrīvatsa mark by those who discourse on Brahman,
because of that which possesses the splendor of the sun, fire, speech, and the moon, being his very own form.
Those who consider themselves masters of speech say that the jewel named Kaustubha exists [therein];
Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, as well as the four-armed Ahaṃkāra, [are present].
The conch, composed of the five elements, situated upon the dust in the hand, is called the mind-wheel (manascakra), ending with the form of a child. || 25 ||
The primordial Māyā is the Śārṅga bow, and the universal lotus rests in my hand;
the primordial Vidyā is the mace (gadā), which is ever-present in my hand as that which is to be known.
The neck is said to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), yet it is adorned by divine armlets of dharma, artha, and kāma, fashioned from the divine and impelled by the primordial *ayajā*.
O Brahmā, Mālā is proclaimed by your mind-born sons;
they call me Kirīṭa, who am immutable and of the nature of pure being (sattva). (28)
One should constantly meditate upon my beloved, who is radiant with a pair of earrings shimmering with an abundance of milk; such a person attains liberation.
He shall be liberated, and I shall indeed grant him my own self;
all this future destiny has been declared by me to you, O Creator.
And its own nature is indeed twofold: consisting of attributes (saguṇa) and devoid of attributes (nirguṇa).
The Lotus-born One said: "How do the ornaments come to be for the manifested forms that have been described? How do the gods sacrifice? How do the Rudras sacrifice?
How does Brahmā sacrifice? How do those born of Brahmā sacrifice? How do the Vināyakas sacrifice? And how do the twelve Ādityas?"

The Vasus sacrifice; the Gandharvas sacrifice; they stand in concealment with their followers. What do humans sacrifice? He said to him: "Indeed, Nārāyaṇa, the primordial God, is the twelve manifest forms in all worlds, in all [beings]."
She abides among all the gods and among humans: as Raudrī among the Rudras, Brāhmī among the Brahmās, Daivī among the gods, Mānavī among humans,
Vighnavināśinī among the Vināyakas, Jyotis among the Ādityas, Gāndharvī among the Gandharvas, and likewise among the Apsarases.

Thus, among the *gaur* [cow-like] powers, the *kāmyā* (desirable) resides in the *suṣu* [wombs/sources], while the *aprakāśinī* (non-shining) resides in the *antardhāna* (disappearances). The *āvirbhāva* (manifestation) and *tirobhāva* (concealment) abide in their own respective places. The *tāmasī*, *rājasī*, *sāttvikī*, and *mānuṣī* [powers] abide in the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), which is a mass of pure consciousness (*vijñānaghana*) and the singular essence of bliss, existence, and consciousness (*ānanda-saccid-ānanda*).
Oṃ, to the Self of Breath, Oṃ, that which is real, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; to that Self of Breath, salutations again and again. || 1 ||
Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇāya Govindāya Gopījanavallabhāya Oṃ Tatsad Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, obeisance again and again to Him. || 2 ||
Oṃ, to the self of the apāna breath, Oṃ tat sat bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, salutations again and again to that self of the apāna breath. || 3 ||
Oṃ, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to Aniruddha, Oṃ, Tat Sat, Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ; to Him indeed, salutations again and again. || 4 ||
Āūṃ, to the self of the pervasive breath (vyāna), Āūṃ, that which is real, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; salutations again and again to that self of the pervasive breath. || 5 ||
Oṃ, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to Rāma, Oṃ, to that which is Tat-Sat-Bhūr-Bhuvaḥ-Suvaḥ, to Him indeed, salutations again and again. || 6 ||
Oṃ, to the self of the udāna breath—Oṃ tat sat bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ—to that self of the udāna breath, salutations again and again. || 7 ||
Oṃ, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the delighter of Devakī, Oṃ tat sat bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, salutations again and again to Him. || 8 ||
Āūṃ, to the Self of the Samāna breath, Āūṃ, to that which is Sat, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ—to that Self of the Samāna breath, salutations again and again! || 9 ||
Oṃ, to the glorious Gopāla, who is one's own true nature, Oṃ tat sat bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 10 ||
Oṃ! He who is that Pradhānātman, Gopāla, Oṃ; to him, who is Tat-sat, Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, salutations again and again. || 11 ||
Oṃ! He who is that very Gopāla, the self of the senses—Oṃ, Tat Sat, Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 12 ||
Oṃ! He who is that very Self of all beings, Gopāla, Oṃ, Tat Sat, Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 13 ||
Oṃ, that which is the Supreme Person, the Cowherd, Oṃ, Tat Sat, Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ; to Him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 14 ||
Oṃ! He who is that Brahman, the supreme Brahman—Oṃ, Tat, Sat, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to Him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 15 ||
Oṃ! He who is the self of all beings, Gopāla, Oṃ—that which is real, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him, salutations again and again. || 16 ||

Oṃ! He who transcends the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turiya), and that which is beyond the fourth; the Inner Controller, Gopāla—Oṃ, *tat sat*, *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*—salutations again and again to Him! 17.
The one God, hidden in all beings,
all-pervading, the inner self of all beings,
the supervisor of actions, and the abode of all beings.
He is the witness, the perceiver, absolute, and devoid of qualities. || 18 ||
Salutation to Rudra. Salutation to Āditya. Salutation to Vināyaka. Salutation to Sūrya. Salutation to Vidyā. Salutation to Indra. Salutation to Agni. Salutation to Yama.
Salutation to Nirṛti. Salutation to Varuṇa. Salutation to Vāyu. Salutation to Kubera.
"Salutations to Īśāna! Salutations to all the gods!
Having offered this most meritorious hymn of praise to Brahmā, who is his own essential nature, he vanished from the sight of all beings. (19)
"O Sage, I heard this from Nārada from Brahmā and the sons of Brahmā;
likewise it was told to me, O Gandharvī: 'Go now to the vicinity of your own abode. (20) Thus [he spoke].
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O worshipful ones.
With steady limbs and bodies, having offered praise, may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unbroken, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace. Hariḥ Oṃ. That is Truth.
Thus ends the Gopālottaratāpinī Upaniṣad.
